Every entry was produced by looking at the image, with the page text for captions. `saw` is the reason for the role; `draft` is the description, applied as a DRAFT narrative that only a person may confirm (bun run narratives). Notable judgements a reviewer may want to revisit: supply-chain img-p019-1 may be the Principles for Digital Development mark (left decorative, unconfirmed); the icons inside its Fig. 30 are decorative because each sits beside a text label that carries the meaning; the reference architecture's two most-repeated images (img-p001-1, img-p019-1) are fully transparent placeholders under the DRAFT watermark; and that draft captions two different figures 'Figure 3.5' (pp. 63 and 77), kept as the document has it. | Bean ay3x (2026-10-03): `vfig-pNNN` entries judge the VECTOR renders pdf-vector-figures.py writes to <entry>/figures/, applied to vector-figures.json by the same script. Each carries its own inspected_by/inspected_at because two of these documents already hold another session's raster verdicts, and `shows` names the declared figures the render holds — the only thing image-descriptions credits. vfig-p015.saw: Fig 5, the seven-phase DIIG planning chart with resource tiles, 'WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture' highlighted
vfig-p015.draft: Fig 5, 'DIIG process for planning and implementing a digital health enterprise'. Seven numbered, colour-coded phases — from 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment to 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. To the right, resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, including the WHO–ITU eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide, the ITU SDG digital investment framework, TOGAF, OpenHIE, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, and the WHO MAPS toolkit. 'WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture (this document)' is highlighted twice: spanning phases 02 to 04, and in phase 07. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

vfig-p032.saw: a boxed TEXT panel — Step 2 'Define a target DHSC architecture' with inputs, tasks, outputs, resources, a best-practice note and a risks table — whose text is in the extracted sections; the page's 'Fig. 14' is a cross-reference and no figure is drawn. Filed as decorative for want of a text-panel role
vfig-p032.draft: Step 2 panel, 'Define a target DHSC architecture': inputs, tasks, outputs and resources boxes, a best-practice note on capturing consumption at the last mile, and a table of potential risks and mitigation strategies.

vfig-p034.saw: Fig 14, the DHSC architecture: services, interoperability layer and supply-chain systems with explanatory callouts
vfig-p034.draft: Fig 14, 'DHSC architecture framework'. Inside a frame labelled DIGITAL HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN ENTERPRISE: SHARED SERVICES (foundational components: facility, product and supplier registries), DATA SERVICES (analytics — supply chain reports, data warehouse; traceability — track and trace, product verification) and Digital ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). Below them, an INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. At the bottom, HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS (forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing), beside EXTERNAL SYSTEMS (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Callouts explain each layer — for example, that OpenHIM is a useful reference for interoperability components, and SCISMM and TSS v2 for the supply chain systems.

vfig-p040.saw: Fig 19, the DHSC architecture with supply-chain information systems split across national, district and facility levels; the page's 'Fig. 20' candidate is a cross-reference
vfig-p040.draft: Fig 19, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: decentralized management (option B)'. The DHSC architecture — shared services, data services, digital ecosystems, an interoperability layer of enabling components, and external systems — with its health supply chain information systems divided by level. At national level: forecasting and planning, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management, warehouse management and cold chain management. At district level: procurement, order management, inventory management and cold chain management. At facility level: dispensing.

vfig-p041.saw: Fig 20, transactional data from a supply-chain flow rising through the interoperability layer into analytics services, with the questions they answer
vfig-p041.draft: Fig 20, 'Benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services'. Along the bottom runs the physical supply chain: manufacturing, shipping, regulatory customs, central-warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional-warehouse replenishment, health-facility dispensing, and patients. Above it sit the planning processes: forecasting and planning; supplier and contract management; procurement; and order management. Dashed arrows carry 'Transactional data from systems relevant to the supply chain' up through the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER into DATA SERVICES — analytics: supply chain reports and a data warehouse. A callout lists the questions analytics services answer: optimizing inventory against consumption to minimize stockouts, whether planned supplies will arrive in time, forecast accuracy against actual consumption, on-time and in-full delivery, wastage and leakage, stock at risk of expiry and where to move it, where and how often stockouts occur, and supplier performance.

vfig-p049.saw: Fig 23, total cost of ownership grouped into implement, scale, operate and ongoing cost components; the crop also takes in the Step 3 text panel above it
vfig-p049.draft: Fig 23, 'Cost components to determine the total cost of ownership'. A dashed loop labelled 'Total cost of ownership' encloses four groups of cost components. IMPLEMENT: sourcing (RFP, RFI, RFQ), software, hardware and infrastructure, design and development, integration and interoperability, testing and training, and deployment. SCALE: expansion of deployment, training, and hardware and infrastructure. OPERATE: software subscriptions, maintenance (personnel, software, hardware), ongoing training, and monitoring and evaluation. ONGOING: management, governance and overhead. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

vfig-p055.saw: Fig 24, supply-chain systems at each location exchanging data through the interoperability layer with traceability services; the page's 'Fig. 25' is a cross-reference
vfig-p055.draft: Fig 24, 'Achieving track and trace capabilities through DHSC architecture components'. Along the bottom, the supply chain runs from regulator through central, regional and district warehouses to health facilities and patients. Each location's system — regulator systems, warehouse management, transportation management, inventory management, dispensing, and verification at the patient — exchanges data in both directions with the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER, as do the external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Above the layer, DATA SERVICES hold analytics and traceability (track and trace, product verification). A callout lists the questions traceability services answer: where a batch is now, whether supply chain integrity was maintained, who had custody on a date, where a batch was dispensed, whether the product moved through known locations, whether there were anomalies, and whether the product is genuine. A legend defines traceability data as what (product, batch and serial number), when, where and why (the transaction type).

vfig-p056.saw: Fig 25, a mock track-and-trace screen for one batch above the event flow that feeds it
vfig-p056.draft: Fig 25, 'Illustrative example of a traceability service interface'. At the top is a mock screen, 'Track and trace results for product 001001123123', batch A1001234. It shows a timeline of five verified events with their location and timestamp: verified and received at the central warehouse (11 Mar 2023); shipped from the central warehouse (5 Apr); verified and received at health facility 001 (6 Apr); verified and dispensed there (10 Apr); and a final patient-side verification of serial number 202 with GPS coordinates (10 Apr, 16:14). Below, the flow that produces it: the manufacturer, central/regional warehouse and health facilities emit ship, receive and dispense events, and handheld verify scans are made along the way. All of these feed DATA SERVICES (analytics and traceability), which answer the screen's query for the product code, batch, its serial numbers 201 to 204 and the expiry date.

img-p030-1.saw: a stepped diagram of product packaging levels
img-p030-1.draft: Fig. 10, 'Product packaging hierarchy' (source: GS1.org), in the section on instituting data management and governance policies. It is drawn as a staircase of four grey steps, each holding packaging illustrations. The top step, labelled PRIMARY, shows individual items such as vials, a bottle, syringes in blister packs, a blister strip and a sterile-packed instrument. The next step, SECONDARY, shows boxes and cartons holding those items; the third, SECONDARY OR TERTIARY, shows open cartons and a row of boxed packs; and the bottom step, TERTIARY, shows shipping cases and a shrink-wrapped pallet of boxes.

vfig-p010.saw: Fig. 1, a health product linked to four circles of product master data; the crop also takes in the section heading and two paragraphs of body prose above it, because the figure's background panel bleeds off the page
vfig-p010.draft: Fig. 1, 'Product master data'. A health product, drawn as a boxed medicine package, is linked to PRODUCT MASTER DATA, shown as four categories with examples. General Information: product identifier, name, description, unit of measure. Classification: ICD, ATC, product characteristics/specifications. Pharmaceutical Information: dosage, strength, route of administration, doses per vial. Logistical Information: packaging, volumetrics, shelf life, storage temperature.

vfig-p011.saw: Fig. 2, partners and processes both feeding a central product-master-data column, flowing down to patients
vfig-p011.draft: Fig. 2, 'Importance of product master data'. Three columns. On the left, SUPPLY CHAIN PARTNERS: manufacturers, procurers, Ministry of Health / programmes, donors, shippers, regulatory authority, central/regional/district warehouses and health facilities. On the right, SUPPLY CHAIN PROCESSES: forecasting and supply planning, procurement, ordering/re-ordering, inventory management, distribution, dispensing, product recalls and finance/insurance. Arrows from both point into the central PRODUCT MASTER DATA column — general information, classification details, pharmaceutical information, logistical information and other information — which flows down through a medicine icon to Patients.

vfig-p012.saw: Fig. 3, the physical flow of products across actors, each system holding a different product code joined by broken links
vfig-p012.draft: Fig. 3, 'Impact of inconsistent product information'. An arrow labelled PHYSICAL FLOW OF HEALTH PRODUCTS runs across five actors: manufacturers, central warehouse, health facilities, community health workers and patients. Beneath them sit the systems each stage uses — a warehouse management system, an eLMIS and paper forms — and each holds the same product under a different code (123123, A1232, P44545, AM545). Broken-chain icons join the codes, showing that the identifiers do not link up along the chain.

vfig-p013.saw: Fig. 4, the seven-phase digital-health planning chart with resource tiles, this document highlighted in phase 07
vfig-p013.draft: Fig. 4, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases — assessing the current state and enabling environment; establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; defining the future state; planning the enterprise architecture; determining health content requirements; M&E and fostering data use; and implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. Resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, among them the DIIG, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, TOGAF, OpenHIE and the WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture. The tile 'WHO handbook for health product catalogue (this document)' is highlighted in phase 07. It is the same chart as Fig. 6 of the WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care, re-pointed to this document.

vfig-p014.saw: Fig. 5, the SMART Guidelines five-layer diagram with localisation and an evidence feedback loop
vfig-p014.draft: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines Approach'. A research and evidence base feeds five knowledge layers and their products: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each passes through LOCALISATION into a country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures, localised requirements, localised machine-readable code and standards, localised static digital services, and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. All feed DATA, EVIDENCE, AND IMPACT, which returns to the evidence base as EVIDENCE FROM DIGITAL IMPLEMENTATIONS.

vfig-p015.saw: Fig. 6, an ANC BPMN swimlane workflow with an enlarged inset of its assessment and counselling activities, some highlighted
vfig-p015.draft: Fig. 6, 'Example of an Antenatal Care Business clinical workflow with highlighted' activities. The upper part is a swimlane process in a health facility, with Client and Health worker lanes. The client arrives at the facility, then goes through registration, rapid assessment and management, a danger-signs/referral decision, pregnancy confirmation, a first-contact decision and a quick check. These lead to collecting the woman's profile and history, then an ANC assessment (check symptoms and follow-up, conduct physical exam, conduct laboratory tests and imaging), then 10. Counselling, in-facility management and treatment, with subactivities 10.1 to 10.9, then a referral decision, scheduling, and self-care in the home or community until the woman returns. The lower part enlarges activities 6 to 10. Highlighted borders mark 9 (conduct laboratory tests and imaging), 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis — the activities that involve health products.

vfig-p016.saw: Fig. 7, a layered architecture with shared/data services, an interoperability layer and supply-chain information systems
vfig-p016.draft: Fig. 7, 'Digital health supply chain architecture framework'. Top row: SHARED SERVICES, whose foundational components are facility, product (highlighted) and supplier registries; DATA SERVICES, with analytics (supply chain reports, data warehouse) and traceability (track and trace, product verification); and Digital Ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). A middle INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. Bottom: HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS — forecasting and planning, order management, warehouse management, cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing — beside External systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories).

vfig-p028.saw: Fig. 8, three columns from classification to product to trade items, with a paracetamol example; the crop clips the rotated row labels at its left edge
vfig-p028.draft: Fig. 8, 'Linkage across classifications, generic products and trade items'. Three columns: CLASSIFICATION (classes or groups of diseases, pathogens or drugs); PRODUCT (name/INN, strength, dosage form, route of administration); and TRADE ITEM (unique identifier such as a GTIN, brand name, manufacturer, country of origin, packaging details, volumetrics, shelf life). The example row traces Nervous system → Analgesics → Other analgesics and antipyretics → Anilides → Paracetamol to the product 'Paracetamol 500 mg tablet'. That product branches into two manufacturers' trade items, each with its own unique IDs and pack hierarchy: a case and inner pack of 100 from ABC Manufacturing (brand Ceta123), and a case, inner pack of 50 and each of 10 from XYZ Manufacturing (brand ParaXYZ). A bottom row gives each column's use: strategic (data aggregation and analysis), tactical (forecasting, procurement planning and aggregate visibility) and operational (inventory, distribution, tracking and tracing, pharmacovigilance and AEFI analysis).

vfig-p029.saw: Fig. 9, a three-class data model with attribute cardinalities and 1-to-0..* associations
vfig-p029.draft: Fig. 9, 'Relationship between generic product, trade item and regulated trade item'. Three classes are drawn as boxes listing their attributes with cardinalities. GENERIC PRODUCT has identifier 0..*, status, name (nameType, nameValue), description, classification, unitOfUse, dosageForm, strength, routeOfAdministration, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, doseQuantity, attribute (type, value[x]) and associatedProduct (product, relationship, quantity). TRADE ITEM has identifier 1..*, status, tradeItemName, description, classification, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, associatedGenericProduct (genericProduct, quantity), contains (tradeItem, quantity) and attribute. REGULATED TRADE ITEM has identifier, status, jurisdiction, authorisationHolder, validityPeriod, authorisedTradeItem, attribute and associatedProduct. The associations read: one generic product to zero or more trade items, and one trade item to zero or more regulated trade items.

vfig-p030.saw: TWO figures, Fig. 10 and Fig. 11, in one crop beneath a WHODrug text panel that the crop also takes in
vfig-p030.draft: Fig. 10, 'Product packaging hierarchy', shows four stepped shelves of packaged goods labelled, top to bottom, PRIMARY (vials, syringes, blister packs), SECONDARY, SECONDARY OR TERTIARY, and TERTIARY (cases and pallets). Source: GS1.org. Fig. 11, 'Example of packaging variations across manufacturers', shows one PRODUCT, a paracetamol 500 mg tablet, procured from two manufacturers with different pack configurations: MFR A ships 1 case of 12 packs of 50 tablets each, and MFR B ships 1 case of 10 packs of 100 tablets each.

vfig-p031.saw: Fig. 12, a generic product linked to manufacturers' trade items through a pallet→case→inner-pack chain; the crop also takes in the next section's 'Step 3' heading band
vfig-p031.draft: Fig. 12, 'Mapping across product packaging hierarchy using FHIR resource'. Five record boxes, each listing identifier, description, name, characteristic and association. A GENERIC PRODUCT (identifier MR001) associates to a trade item from manufacturer A (identifier 17801415202675) and to manufacturer B's tertiary pallet (18901415202906). The pallet associates to MFR B's tertiary case (08901415202908, quantity 100), which associates to MFR B's secondary inner pack (08901415202910, quantity 50) — the packaging hierarchy expressed as chained associations.

vfig-p040.saw: Fig. 13, a national product code record branching to two GTIN/trade-item tables; whole page checked at low resolution and the crop holds the whole figure
vfig-p040.draft: Fig. 13, 'Transitional approach to adopting globally unique trade item numbers'. A national product code record — NPC01101001, Lamivudine 50 mg tablet, dosage form TA, route oral — branches into two tables of trade items mapped to it. The first holds GS1 GTINs (for example 58904093825793) for manufacturer MFR001 from IN, with child GTINs, child quantities of 100 and 10, 3000 eaches and a shelf life of 670. The second holds items from MFR002 from KE that have no GTIN yet and are identified only by country trade item identifiers (P006008, P006009), with child quantities of 120 and 30, 7200 eaches and a shelf life of 1095. So a national code can carry GTIN-identified and not-yet-GTIN-identified items side by side during the transition.

vfig-p041.saw: only the header band of a text table (POTENTIAL RISKS / MITIGATION); the page's 'Figure 11' and 'Figure 12' are cross-references, and no figure is drawn here
vfig-p041.draft: Header band of a two-column table, reading 'POTENTIAL RISKS' and 'MITIGATION'.

vfig-p046.saw: Fig. 14, a global catalogue feeding two country catalogues inside the PCMT on WHO infrastructure
vfig-p046.draft: Fig. 14, 'Illustration of how countries can leverage WHO hosted PCMT'. Inside a panel labelled PRODUCT CATALOGUE MANAGEMENT TOOL, a GLOBAL CATALOGUE (global identifier, unit of use, pharmaceutical information such as dosage form, route of administration and strength, trade item information, and manufacturer, country of origin and shelf life) feeds COUNTRY CATALOGUE A and COUNTRY CATALOGUE B, each adding country identifiers and country-specific information such as registration numbers. The arrows are annotated 'Country catalogues to derive common product information from the global catalog'. Country A Users and Country B Users each work in their own catalogue, and the whole sits on WHO INFRASTRUCTURE.

vfig-p050.saw: Fig. 15, Fig. 14's PCMT diagram extended with product master data flowing back into the global catalogue from countries
vfig-p050.draft: Fig. 15, 'Illustration of how countries can share data with the WHO hosted PCMT'. It extends Fig. 14. As there, the global catalogue feeds country catalogues A and B inside the PRODUCT CATALOGUE MANAGEMENT TOOL on WHO infrastructure, used by Country A and Country B users. In addition, each country catalogue returns 'Product master data' to the global catalogue, and OTHER COUNTRIES contribute PRODUCT MASTER DATA into it from above, so the global catalogue is fed by the countries as well as feeding them.

img-p041-2.saw: Figure 2.2 infographic of REDDHI: purpose, why resilient/essential, STAC foundations, role, objectives, principles
img-p041-2.draft: Figure 2.2, 'REDDHI: resilient and essential dimensions, the full-STAC foundations, and REDDHI's role within national digital architecture' (section 2.2, Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health Infrastructure). Headed 'Resilient Essential Data & Digital Health Infrastructure', it describes REDDHI as a direction of travel rather than a fixed destination. It explains 'Why resilient' (survives funding volatility, reduces external vendor dependency, long-term technical sustainability, builds local capacity) and 'Why essential' (minimum capabilities, a foundation for multiple use cases, investment efficiency, a subset of the broader national architecture). A band 'Built on open full-STAC foundations' has four parts: Standards (HL7 FHIR, ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC, CQL), Technologies (open-source tooling and SDKs), Architectures (DPI-based, modular, plug-and-play) and Content (WHO SMART Guidelines). Further bands give REDDHI's role (a subset of the whole, connected to foundational DPI, governed for interoperability), five objectives (transition from fragmentation, build governed and interoperable foundations, enable local and regional innovation, ensure technical and financial sustainability, position countries for large-scale investment) and nine guiding principles.

img-p048-2.saw: Figure 2.3 semicircular diagram of the ten DPI-H architecture design principles with icons and definitions
img-p048-2.draft: Figure 2.3, 'DPI-H Architecture Design Principles' (section 2.3). A semicircle of ten blue segments, each with an icon, surrounds the central title. Each principle has a one-line definition: Governance, Open Standards, Interoperability, Sustainability, Modularity, Local Capacity, Equity and Inclusion, Data Ownership, Access and Control, Trust and Security, and Ethics. For example, Modularity is 'building loosely coupled components that can be introduced, replaced, and improved incrementally', and Interoperability is 'designing for meaningful data exchange across systems and foundational DPI from the outset'.

img-p059-2.saw: Figure 3.2 full layered integrated view of the DPI-H reference architecture, goals through technology, with an interoperability column
img-p059-2.draft: Figure 3.2, the DPI-H reference architecture as a layered integrated view (section 3.3, The reference architecture in practice). Top to bottom: Strategic Health Goals G1 to G7 (Trusted data foundations, Health workforce, Quality and continuity of care, Personal health record, Supply chain, Health financing, Climate and epidemic resilience); a Cross-cutting Governance band (Policy, legislation and regulation; Cybersecurity, privacy and consent; Standards, certification and conformance; Semantic governance and stewardship; Auditability, assurance and accountability); Stakeholders, such as citizens, health workforce, government/MoH, facilities, financial entities, suppliers, development agencies and research; and Capabilities, such as identity management, access/consent/trust, health record management, knowledge management, clinical services and care coordination, health workforce management, health financing, supply chain, analytics and BI, and climate and public-health surveillance. Next is the Point-of-Service and Functional Applications layer, which the private sector, donors, NGOs and implementers build: provider systems, case management, pharmacy, CHW and community, citizen/patient apps, supply chain, health coverage and claims, financing and workforce operations, and public health apps. These consume the DPI-H layer through standards-based APIs. The DPI-H layer, government-stewarded reusable infrastructure, holds Reusable Components (Clinical services with a Computable Decision Support Engine, Supply chain with a Supplier Registry, Health financing with a Benefits Package Registry, Public health and analytics with a PH Surveillance Platform and HMIS, AI-enabled intelligence, and Secondary use). It also holds a Shared Data Layer of core registries, several starred as REDDHI components: Client Registry, Lifelong Health Record, Health Workforce Registry, Facility Registry, Product Registry, Terminology Service and Logical Information Model Repository. Below these come the Foundational DPI Layer (DPI-F: foundational identity, national trust services, payment rails, data exchange fabric, CRVS and other sectors, geo-location and notification) and the Technology Layer (hybrid/sovereign cloud, AI/ML platform, security and trust operations, data platform, observability/DevSecOps). A cross-cutting Interoperability column on the right holds an Information Mediator (API gateway, HIE), open standards (such as HL7 FHIR, IHE, openEHR, IPS, SNOMED CT, ICD-11, LOINC, GS1, CDS Hooks, SMART on FHIR, OpenID/OAuth2, DICOM) and integration patterns (REST APIs, event streams, IHE documents, federated query, bulk data, cross-border IHR/IPS). It connects to each layer through interface markers.

img-p061-2.saw: Figure 3.3 ArchiMate goal-to-component view for the Trusted Personal Health Record goal
img-p061-2.draft: Figure 3.3, 'Simplified view of a single health goal (Establish Trusted Personal Health Records)' (section 3.3). At the top, a 'TPHR Goals' group holds the overall goal of a secure, universally accessible system for issuing verifiable digital health records. It is composed of four sub-goals: a verifiable health record for every individual; patient control and consent-based sharing; trust, security and privacy in all transactions; and interoperability across providers, facilities and jurisdictions. A 'TPHR Outcomes' group lists four outcomes, such as citizens empowered to own, access and share their health records. These realise the goals. A 'TPHR Implementation' area shows capabilities realising those outcomes, including Health Record Management, Identity and Authentication, Universal Access Enablement, Dynamic Consent Management, Data Governance, Data Sharing and Authorization, Audit and Compliance Monitoring, Trust and Verification, Data Privacy, Incident Detection and Response, Interoperability and Health Information Exchange, Terminology and Data Management, and Provider and Facility Verification. Below them, application services such as Client Identity Service, Consent Management Service, FHIR API Service and Terminology Service (SNOMED, ICD, LOINC) are realised by application components such as Lifelong Health Record, Client Registry, PHR Portal/Mobile App, PKI/Trust Infrastructure, IAM/Access Control System, SIEM, Interoperability Middleware, Terminology Service and Facility Registry.

img-p062-2.draft: Figure 3.4, 'Layered view for one sub-goal relating to Establish Trusted Personal Health Records' (section 3.3). The sub-goal 'Establish a secure, universally accessible, verifiable health record for every individual' is realised by the outcome 'Population has verifiable digital health records'. Within 'TPHR Sub-goal #1 Implementation', three capabilities realise that outcome: Health Record Management, Identity and Authentication, and Universal Access Enablement. img-p063-2.draft: Figure 3.5 on page 52, 'Layered view for one sub-goal relating to ensuring Quality and Continuity of Care' (section 3.3). img-p072-2.saw: Figure 3.4.2 terminology services maturity model chart, from Nascent to Data Exchange
img-p072-2.draft: Figure 3.4.2, 'A terminology maturity spectrum, from minimal reference-list management to a fully governed, multi-stakeholder ecosystem', adapted from the OpenHIE Terminology Service maturity model (section 3.4.5). A rising line plots five maturity levels: Nascent (no centrally defined content or governance); Emerging (some centrally defined content in non-standard formats, with limited adoption and governance); Shared Electronic Reference (up-to-date definitions aligned across key programmes); Digital Subscription (key systems subscribe electronically to the central service to stay up to date); and Data Exchange (the terminology service automates information exchange, for example code validation and value set expansion). Red break marks between Emerging and Shared Electronic Reference show a steep climb. A callout notes that many LMICs are at early stages and that this step needs a different way of doing business. Braces underneath group the first three levels as emphasising selection, definition and governance of standards, and the last two as emphasising use of terminologies for data exchange.

img-p073-2.saw: Figure 3.4.3 NHDD stacked-layer diagram of hierarchical terminology content with top-down and feedback arrows
img-p073-2.draft: Figure 3.4.3, 'Hierarchical terminology content, from global reference standards to facility-level dictionaries, with top-down customisation and upward feedback', adapted from the OpenHIE National Health Data Dictionary (NHDD) framework (section 3.4.5). Titled 'NHDD Framework: Content Structure', it stacks five layers from top to bottom: Reference/Administrative Code Sets (for example SNOMED, ICD, HL7); Curated Concept Sources/Interface Terminologies (for example CIEL, IMO); Country-level Subsets/Customizations; Organization-level Dictionaries/Customizations; and Facility-level Dictionaries (for example formularies). A downward arrow on the left says that international standards are selected and customised for country use, then adapted further for local implementation. An upward arrow on the right reads 'Submissions / Feedback to Standards' and 'Responsive Local & National Governance'.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig. 1.1.1 (landscape page), the seven-phase planning chart with resource tiles, the DIIG itself highlighted spanning phases 02–05
vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 1.1.1, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven colour-coded phases — 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 defining the future state; 04 planning the enterprise architecture; 05 determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. Resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked PDF or online. vfig-p019.saw: Fig. 1.1.4, a flow from strategy through roadmap and architecture to applications and scale, with the DIIG's scope boxed; the crop also takes in Box 1.1.3 and the body prose above it
vfig-p019.draft: Fig. 1.1.4, 'Essential processes of national digital health implementations'. A left-to-right flow runs DIGITAL HEALTH STRATEGY → INVESTMENT ROADMAP → ENTERPRISE ARCHITECTURE → APPLICATION WITH INTERVENTIONS → SCALE, INSTITUTIONALIZE AND SUSTAIN, with a feedback arrow from scaling back to applications. Inputs feed in from above: national health priorities (into the strategy), the national inventory of digital assets (exchanged with the roadmap and architecture) and health-programme-specific needs. Governance mechanisms and a data use culture support from below, and the digital maturity of the country informs the strategy. A shaded region labelled DIIG encloses the architecture, applications and scaling steps — the part this guide covers. At the bottom sit the national eHealth strategy building blocks: leadership and governance; strategy and investment; legislation, policy and compliance; workforce; infrastructure; standards and interoperability; and services and applications.

vfig-p043.saw: Fig. 3.1, three columns — Think, Rethink, Describe — for analysis, redesign and requirements; the caption itself sits outside the crop
vfig-p043.draft: Fig. 3.1, 'Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges' and requirements. Three columns. BUSINESS PROCESS ANALYSIS, 'Think — how do we do our work now?': define goals and objectives, determine the health programme processes to target, map the user journey and workflow, and identify pain points. BUSINESS PROCESS REDESIGN, 'Rethink — how should we do our work now?': examine tasks and workflow, identify inefficiencies, restructure them, and select digital health interventions for the prioritized health system challenges. REQUIREMENTS DEFINITION, 'Describe — how can an information system support our work?': define the tasks for the optimized processes, describe how business rules are implemented, check that the enabling environment can support the interventions, define what the interventions should do from end-user needs, and determine whether existing ICT systems can be leveraged.

vfig-p044.saw: Fig. 3.1.1.1, a process matrix table; the crop also takes in the section heading and body prose. NOTE: the caption says 'three example processes' but the table holds FOUR (A–D) — a discrepancy in the source, recorded rather than corrected
vfig-p044.draft: Fig. 3.1.1.1, 'Process matrix illustrating three example processes within a typical vaccination programme'. A table with the columns Process, Objective, Task set and Outcomes, holding four rows. A Patient management keeps a database of all newborns and their vaccination history (register, search, maintain), leading to more complete registration. B Vaccination management ensures every infant receives all scheduled doses (define the schedule, plan, send reminders, register vaccinations, monitor coverage), leading to more timely vaccination and higher coverage. C Stock management keeps vaccines available while minimizing wastage (order, receive, store, count, monitor balances and expiry), leading to higher availability and lower wastage. D Service delivery ensures quality vaccination services (counsel, diagnose, dispense, refer, update the record, schedule the next visit), leading to correct protocol, timelier vaccinations and better documentation.

vfig-p057.saw: Fig. 4.1, the Think/Rethink/Describe chart of Fig. 3.1 with the redesign and requirements columns boxed as 'Chapter 4'; the caption sits outside the crop
vfig-p057.draft: Fig. 4.1, 'Redesigning health programme processes'. It repeats the three-column chart of Fig. 3.1: business process analysis ('Think — how do we do our work now?'), business process redesign ('Rethink — how should we do our work now?') and requirements definition ('Describe — how can an information system support our work?'), each with its tasks. Here the redesign and requirements columns are boxed together under the label 'Chapter 4', marking the part of the approach the chapter covers.

vfig-p064.saw: Fig. 4.2.1, the eHealth building blocks grouped into enabling and ICT environments, each with its contributions
vfig-p064.draft: Fig. 4.2.1, 'Roles and contributions of component “building blocks”' to a national eHealth environment. Two groups of building blocks, each block paired with its contributions. ENABLING ENVIRONMENT: leadership, governance and multisector engagement (direct and coordinate eHealth nationally, align with health goals, support change); strategy and investment (a responsive national strategy and plan, with financing aligned to priorities); legislation, policy and compliance (national policies and a legal and enforcement environment that builds trust); workforce (eHealth knowledge and skills, networks, and education and training programmes); and standards and interoperability (consistent, accurate collection and exchange of health information). ICT ENVIRONMENT: infrastructure (networks, core services and applications for information exchange across boundaries) and services and applications (the means of delivering health content and managing information, for the public, patients, providers and others).

vfig-p073.saw: Fig. 4.5.1, a five-row checklist of design considerations, each with its guiding questions; the caption sits outside the crop
vfig-p073.draft: Fig. 4.5.1, 'Considerations for designing a digital health enterprise'. A checklist of five ticked considerations, each with guiding questions. Identified pain points and health system challenges: what challenges did the stakeholders identify, and are digital interventions appropriate or should non-digital approaches also be considered? Evidence base and experience with the digital health intervention(s): has it been shown to address the challenges, will more than one be needed, and has it been tested at the necessary scale? Enabling environment: can the enabling and ICT environment support it, and what precautions are needed (see Chapter 5)? Requirements: how well does the enterprise meet user needs and stakeholder expectations, and does it fit the existing culture, language and workflows? Linkages to other ICT enterprises: are other interventions being implemented in the context, and can they be leveraged?

vfig-p078.saw: Fig. 5.1 — health content plus interventions giving applications, resting on the seven building blocks — and the crop also takes in body prose and the top of Table 5.2, which is drawn in vector beneath it
vfig-p078.draft: Fig. 5.1, 'Essential components of a digital health implementation'. Across the top: HEALTH CONTENT (information aligned with recommended health practices) + DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTIONS (discrete functions of digital technology for health-sector objectives) → DIGITAL APPLICATIONS (software and communication channels that deliver them, supported by shared services). Dotted lines tie this to the SERVICES & APPLICATIONS block of a foundational layer, 'ICT and Enabling Environment', made of the building blocks: leadership and governance across the top, above strategy and investment; services and applications; standards and interoperability; infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance; and workforce.

vfig-p101.saw: Fig. 6.3.2, the OpenHIE layered architecture with a numbered ten-item legend; the crop also takes in Box 6.3.1 above it
vfig-p101.draft: Fig. 6.3.2, 'OpenHIE architectural diagram illustrating mechanisms for interoperability across different applications'. Within a DIGITAL HEALTH PLATFORM, the OpenHIE component layer holds business domain services — (1) logistics management information system, (2) shared health record and (3) health management information system — and registry services — (4) terminology services, (5) client registry, (6) facility registry, (7) health worker registry and (8) product registry. Beneath them, (9) the interoperability services layer provides authentication, an interlinking service and entity mapping. Below the platform sit (10) point-of-service applications: mobile system, electronic medical record, health management information system, lab, pharmacy and logistics management information system. A legend defines each numbered component — for example, that the interoperability layer receives all communications from external services and orchestrates data exchange with the component layer. Adapted from OpenHIE architecture v2, 2019.

vfig-p133.saw: Fig. 9.2, four interlocking puzzle pieces for policy, technical, institutional and financial sustainability; the crop holds the whole BID Initiative case-study panel around it
vfig-p133.draft: Fig. 9.2, 'Critical sustainability elements'. Four interlocking puzzle pieces, each annotated. POLICY: understand the country's policy environment, including gaps in existing policies and strategies. TECHNICAL: map government capacity to manage solutions over the long term, and develop a capacity-building plan for human skills and infrastructure. INSTITUTIONAL: identify the level of engagement and participation across the health system in the design and adaptation of solutions. vfig-p015.saw: Fig. 1, a staircase diagram above a four-column comparison table
vfig-p015.draft: Fig. 1, 'From paper to digital: a transformational journey'. The upper half is a rising staircase of four stages, each an icon and a heading — PAPER, DIGITIZATION, DIGITALIZATION, DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION — joined by arrows labelled 'From paper to digital', 'Improve existing processes' and 'Fundamentally change healthcare delivery'. A vertical axis, 'Data use', runs from 'Limited data use with little to no interoperability standards adopted' at the bottom to 'Greater data use with greater adoption of interoperability standards' at the top; a horizontal arrow beneath is labelled 'Process Optimization'. The lower half is a table with one column per stage (Paper, Digitization, Digitalization, Digital transformation) and five rows: Definition, Examples, Benefits, Challenges and Dependencies. For example, Paper is defined as manually capturing and processing data in paper formats, with examples such as paper register books and tally sheets; Digital transformation is defined as digitally optimizing and driving systems-level change through innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms, with examples such as algorithms for personalized treatment plans.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig. 3, four nested rounded layers around the care seeker with digital-solution icons in each
vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 3, 'Delivering an integrated ecosystem of information systems and digital health solutions supports the PHC approach'. Four nested layers surround a figure labelled 'Centered around the needs of the care seeker'. From innermost to outermost: COMMUNITY LINKAGES AND ENGAGEMENT (community health workers, care seekers) holds patient portal, targeted messaging, CHW job aid, self-monitoring devices and capacity building; ORGANIZATION AND MANAGEMENT (primary care providers) holds clinical job aids, AI risk assessment, referral and coordination, and an electronic health record; SELECTION, DESIGN AND PLANNING OF SERVICES (health system decision makers) holds a dashboard and management information systems; DEFINING A TARGET POPULATION AND UNDERSTANDING THEIR NEEDS (policy makers) holds civil registration and vital statistics, and disease surveillance. Each solution carries a one-line purpose. A note says solutions can span more than one layer and are allocated to one only for illustration.

vfig-p019.saw: Fig. 4, a five-tier stack of data uses with a person at the base
vfig-p019.draft: Fig. 4, 'The added value of “collect once, use for many purposes” principle'. Five stacked tiers rise from a person icon at the base. Bottom to top: Primary, individual data collection (clinical, lab, pharmacy, registries and ID data); Person-centred health service delivery (clinical decision support, scheduling, case management); Programme management (operational decision support, quality improvement, facility management, process optimization); Health system monitoring (national strategic plans and policies, national indicators, accountability); and Global monitoring (accountability towards the SDGs). A side bar groups the lower two tiers as 'Primary data use' and the upper three as 'Secondary data use'.

vfig-p020.saw: Fig. 5, five knowledge layers L1–L5 flowing through localisation to country adaptation
vfig-p020.draft: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines approach'. A 'Research and evidence base' bar feeds five knowledge layers, each with its product: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each layer passes through a 'Localisation' bar into a matching country-implementation adaptation: national policies and guidelines (L1), localised requirements (L2), localised machine-readable code and standards (L3), localised static digital services (L4) and dynamic digital applications optimised for local outcomes (L5). All five feed 'Data, evidence, and impact', which loops back to the evidence base as 'Evidence from digital implementations'.

vfig-p024.saw: Fig. 6, seven colour-coded phases with steps and a grid of linked resources
vfig-p024.draft: Fig. 6, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases run down the left: 01 Assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 Establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 Defining the future state; 04 Planning the enterprise architecture; 05 Determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 Implementing, maintaining and scaling. Each phase lists its steps, for example 'Develop a national digital health strategy' in phase 02 and 'Identify validated health content appropriate for the implementation context' in phase 05. To the right, resource tiles are placed against the phase(s) they serve, some spanning several phases, and each is marked as a PDF for print or an online environment. They include the WHO–ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits and machine-readable recommendations, TOGAF, Open HIE, ICD-11, HL7 FHIR, LOINC, the WHO MAPS toolkit and Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. The tile 'WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care (this document)' sits in phase 05.

vfig-p026.saw: Fig. 7, three successive iteration loops along a release arrow
vfig-p026.draft: Fig. 7, 'Iterative and agile approach'. Three circular loops sit along a horizontal timeline arrow: Minimum viable product (MVP), then VERSION 1, then VERSION 2. Each loop has the same four stages: understand and prioritize user requirements, design (adapt design in later versions), build and test, and train users. Milestones along the arrow read: determine that a PCPOSS is an appropriate health intervention; repeat the previous loop until meeting MVP specs to deploy; deploy and roll out; gather and manage user feedback; deploy and roll out; gather and manage user feedback; deploy, roll out and scale; and iterations for continuous improvement.

vfig-p032.saw: Fig. 8, an inverted pyramid of interview stages from broad to narrow with example prompts
vfig-p032.draft: Fig. 8, 'Example prompts and questions for starting broad and narrowing down'. An inverted pyramid of four bands runs from BROAD (start here) at the top to NARROW (end here) at the tip: TRUST BUMP, BIRD'S EYE VIEW, MAGNIFYING GLASS and MICRO-SCOPE. Beside each band are example interview prompts for health workers: intent and introductions ('Tell me about your background… as a health worker'); 'Tell me about the last time you… registered a new client / provided antenatal care / provided a routine immunization to a child'; 'Can you tell me more… about how you check for malaria?' and 'Can you show me how you… would fill out a paper register now?'; and the 5 Whys ('Why do you… wait until the end of the day to fill out your records?'), continued until a root cause is revealed. It closes with 'Express gratitude for health worker's time'. Adapted from Tran, 2018, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

vfig-p035.saw: Fig. 9, a five-column table of family-planning business processes A–C
vfig-p035.draft: Fig. 9, 'Example business process matrix from family planning DAK'. A table with the columns Process name, Process ID, Personas, Objectives and Task set, the header row defining each column. Three processes follow. A Registration (FP.A), with client and clerk or health-care provider, ensures the client is in the system and queued for counselling; its tasks are to search for, review and update, or create a client record. B Family planning counselling (FP.B), with client and health-care provider, discusses methods and selects one the client is medically eligible for; its tasks run from taking a history and a risk assessment through checking medical eligibility criteria and stock to referral if the facility cannot provide the method. C Service provision (FP.C) provides the chosen method, covering informed consent, start timing, dual protection and follow-up scheduling. Source: WHO (30).

vfig-p038.saw: TWO figures on one page — the Fig. 10 swimlane workflow and the Fig. 11 annotation panel — and the crop also takes in the body prose and a TIP box between and below them, because their drawn frames span the page
vfig-p038.draft: Fig. 10, 'Workflow A: Registration business process', is a BPMN-style swimlane diagram. The pool is 'Health facility', with lanes Client and Health worker or Clerk. The client arrives at the facility (1), then rapid assessment and management (2) leads to 'Urgent referral necessary?' (3); Yes ends in C. ANC referral. No leads to gather client details (4), then search for client (5) and 'Match found?' (6). No leads to create client record (7); Yes leads to a grouped subprocess 8, Validate client details: review sociodemographic data with the client (8.1), 'Update needed?' (8.2), then update client details (8.3). Both paths reach check-in client (9), ending in B. ANC contact. Fig. 11, 'Notes and annotations for Workflow A: Registration business process', is a three-column text panel that annotates each numbered activity of Fig. 10 — for example, that rapid assessment is outside the DAK's scope, and the identifiers a client may present when searched for. Both cite WHO (29).

vfig-p042.saw: Fig. 12, a three-question flow with explanation and action columns
vfig-p042.draft: Fig. 12, 'Is each and every data element collected truly needed?'. Three rows, each reading Question → Explanation → Action to be taken, with arrows chaining each row's action into the next question. 1. Is the data element duplicated? Duplicates may share a definition under different labels, or be collected on several forms; reconcile them into one element collected once. 2. Is the data element needed for service delivery or accountability? Ask whether it supports clinical decision-making, mandatory reporting or accountability; if not, consider removing it to reduce the data-entry burden on health workers. 3. Is the data element orphaned? Orphaned data is hard to use without its context; link it to its primary data elements (anything not needed will already have gone at question 2).

vfig-p045.draft: Fig. 13, 'Example decision-support logic matrix from DAK for HIV'. A table with four columns: activity ID and name, decision table ID, decision table description, and reference/source. It has six rows, HIV.DT.01 to HIV.DT.06: check for serious illness; test for HIV using the testing algorithm; determine retest recommendation; PrEP eligibility check; determine PEP or PrEP regimen; and screen for TB. Each row cites the WHO consolidated guideline section it is drawn from — for example the 2019 consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, and its figures on universal HIV testing and early infant diagnosis. Source: WHO (31).

vfig-p046.saw: Fig. 14, a branching decision tree from antenatal registration on HIV status and risk
vfig-p046.draft: Fig. 14, 'Decision-support logic for a clinical care pathway in the form of a decision tree'. It starts at 'Antenatal registration — provider-initiated HIV testing & counselling' and splits on the result. HIV-positive leads to PMTCT, treatment, support and an offer of partner notification, then partner testing. Partner HIV-negative leads to reassessing the woman's risk and offering partner referral for VMMC. Partner not tested or HIV-positive leads to offering the partner HIV treatment (if positive), condom promotion and risk-reduction counselling. HIV-negative leads to standard post-test guidance and counselling on prevention, then two branches: offer partner testing and a risk assessment (which feeds partner testing), and a risk assessment using a tool. That tool separates a woman at substantial risk of HIV acquisition from one who is not. At substantial risk, she is offered comprehensive prevention options — STI screening and treatment, condom promotion, risk-reduction counselling, PrEP with emphasis on adherence, and follow-up ANC visits. A woman who chooses to initiate PrEP then receives clinical laboratory assessments, adherence counselling, and emphasis on follow-up visits and repeat HIV testing. Source: WHO (29).

vfig-p054.saw: Fig. 15, three coloured phases on fidelity-versus-time axes with questions under each
vfig-p054.draft: Fig. 15, 'Levels of insight gained from different prototypes'. The vertical axis is level of prototype fidelity and the horizontal axis is the time required to develop the protocol. An arrow climbs through three phases: Validation, with low-fidelity prototypes (sketches, wireframes); Refinement, with moderate-fidelity prototypes (mockups); and Deployment, with higher-fidelity prototypes (clickable prototypes). Under each phase are the questions it answers. Validation asks: do users need this, and would this digital record solve their administrative reporting problems? Refinement asks: could it improve service delivery or accountability, and will users use it as intended? Deployment asks: does it have the key features, will users adopt it, and what behaviour change or roadblocks to adoption must be addressed? Adapted from Norman Tran/Stanford school (35).
